claims.source: Salas, Great Falls Tribune interview (1996); signed affidavit published by Robert Hastings; 'Faded Giant' (2005)
claims.text: Salas states that while on duty in a Minuteman launch control capsule at Malmstrom in March 1967 he received a report from topside security police of a glowing red object over the front gate, and that his flight's missiles then went off alert.
Col. Frederick Meiwald, Salas's commander, wrote to Salas on 1 October 1996 concerning the incident; the letter is published in facsimile.
Salas signed an affidavit on the incident which Robert Hastings publishes in facsimile.

conflicts: A later investigation attributes the loss of power and the visual report to a nearby test of an electromagnetic pulse simulator. James Carlson, son of the Echo Flight commander, has publicly disputed Salas's account. Salas has additionally claimed a 1985 abduction from his home, which is a separate and ungradeable claim and is not relied on here.

label: Capt. Robert L. Salas
narrative: Robert L. Salas is the named officer at the centre of the Malmstrom March 1967 missile shutdown claim. A US Air Force Academy graduate with a master's in aerospace engineering from the Air Force Institute of Technology, he served seven years on active duty as an ICBM launch controller and missile propulsion engineer, resigned his commission in 1971, worked at Martin Marietta and Rockwell International, then spent two decades at the Federal Aviation Administration to about 1995. He first went on the record in a 1996 interview with the Great Falls Tribune: while on duty in a launch control capsule at Malmstrom he took a call from a topside Air Force security police officer reporting a glowing red object hovering over the front gate, and within moments the missiles in his flight went off alert status one after another. He has repeated the account in a signed affidavit held by Robert Hastings, in his books 'Faded Giant' (2005, with James Klotz) and 'Unidentified' (2014), at the 27 September 2010 National Press Club event, and in the 2025 documentary 'The Age of Disclosure'. His most important corroboration is a letter from his commander, Col. Frederick Meiwald, dated 1 October 1996, published in facsimile by Hastings. Salas is also the case where this board's grading discipline bites hardest in both directions: the underlying fact that a Malmstrom flight of ten Minuteman missiles went off alert in March 1967 is documented in Air Force paper, while the causal attribution to an aerial object is testimony, and a competing engineering explanation - a nearby electromagnetic pulse simulator test - has been advanced against it.
